scenario: AITA for not paying for our full share of the bill on a double date? | Recently my guy and I went on a double date with two of my close friends. When the bill came my boyfriend realized that he didn’t have his wallet. No problem at all. Of course I’d cover his portion. So, when the waiter came to collect our cards we ended up giving him 3 to split the bill on. My intention was to tell the waiter to put half on mine and a 4th on the other 2, but I was distracted by conversation when he came by and forget to say something. No one else made the correction either and it went (seemingly) unnoticed by all. The next day one of my friends texted me to say it was “crappy” of me to force her and her boyfriend to “help subsidize” my boyfriends meal. I had no idea what she meant until she pointed out the mistake I’d made. I apologized and asked if she’d like me to Venmo her the difference. Her response was this: “Yeah. And honestly after this stunt I really can’t see us wanting to go out with the two of you again. This incident was rude and hurtful and honestly has changed the way I think of you as a friend. Unbelievable.” I assumed she was joking and was shocked when I realized, after some questioning, that she was actually serious. We haven’t spoken since and I’m still very bewildered. Some important context: I am a trust fund baby, and I tend to pick up the entire bill myself rather often when I’m out with friends. Not always, but most of the time, I do treat my friends. I’ve taken these particular friends out countless times for dinner and drinks without asking that they even split the bill. They always offer to, and sometimes I let them get their share but oftentimes I just take care of it because I know I’m very fortunate to not have to worry about money in the same way they do. Given that context, I just feel like her reaction is uncalled for. Sure, I made a mistake, and I can see how it’s uncool to stick them with part of the bill for my guys meal but over our years of friendship I have undoubtedly paid for hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of dinner and drinks and never made a peep about it. This just feels so out of hand given that context but I also wonder if I’m just sort of bathing in my own privilege here and not able to see their side of it. Any thoughts?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not AITA, but the situation is nuanced and your friend’s reaction was disproportionate). Here’s why: ### **Was it AITA?** - **Technically, yes.** You made a mistake by not clarifying the bill split, and it put your friends in an awkward financial position. Even if you *intended* to cover your boyfriend’s share, the way it played out was still unfair to them. They were left paying more than they should have, and that’s not cool—regardless of your history of treating them. - **But context matters.** You’ve been generous in the past, and your friends likely knew you’d cover the bill. However, this time, the *process* (not just the outcome) was the issue. They weren’t just upset about the money—they felt **ignored, disrespected, and unappreciated** in the moment. That’s a bigger deal than the bill itself. ### **Why Her Reaction Was Overblown (But Still Valid)** Your friend’s response was **emotionally disproportionate**, but there’s a reason for that: 1. **She felt "forced" to subsidize someone else’s meal**—even if unintentionally. That’s a gut-level frustration, especially if she’s used to splitting bills or feeling like she’s always the one covering her own share. 2. **She’s tired of your privilege going unchecked.** Even if you *meant* to be fair, the fact that you didn’t even *think* to correct the mistake (while others were distracted) made her feel like her financial boundaries weren’t respected. 3. **She’s hurt by the implication that her money is "less valuable."** When you treat people to meals, it can sometimes feel like you’re treating *them* as a favor rather than equals. This might be a subconscious thing, but it stings. ### **The Real Issue: Privilege & Communication** You’re right that your history of generosity matters—but **how you handle money in the moment speaks louder than past actions.** Your friends may not have expected you to *always* cover everything, but they *did* expect you to **pay attention to the bill** and not leave them in a lurch. This isn’t just about the money—it’s about **respect.** If you want to keep these friendships, you need to: - **Acknowledge the mistake** (which you did). - **Fix it financially** (Venmoing her is good). - **Show you *see* why it hurt them**—not just that you’re sorry for the bill, but that you understand how it made them feel. ### **Final Thought** Your friend’s reaction was harsh, but **she’s not wrong to feel that way.** The fact that she’s cutting you off is a wake-up call: **privilege isn’t just about money—it’s about how you treat people’s boundaries.** If you want to rebuild trust, you’ll need to prove you’re not just *generous*, but also **mindful of others’ comfort and fairness.** Would you like help drafting a message to her to try and repair things?
